Oh, wow, yeah. Absolutely. I mean, I remember this starting way, way before high school. Actually, it’s funny you ask about being younger than twelve, because my mom used to keep all my old report cards and teacher evaluations in this big binder, and every single parent-teacher conference in elementary school was pretty much the exact same conversation. 

They would always write these notes saying that I was a really bright kid, which, you know, is nice to hear, but then there was always a "but." It was always, "she’s bright, but she rushes through everything." And the talking! I was constantly getting in trouble for talking out of turn. I just couldn't seem to hold my thoughts in—if the teacher asked a question, I’d just blurt out the answer before she even finished calling on someone else, or I'd be chatting with the kid next to me when we were supposed to be doing silent reading. 

And the homework situation was a constant battle. I was always forgetting my homework. Half the time I’d actually do it at home, but then I’d leave it on the kitchen counter, or I'd forget to even write down what the assignment was in the first place. And my desk... oh my gosh, my desk in like, third and fourth grade was a complete disaster zone. If you lifted the top, it was just stuffed to the absolute brim with half-finished papers, crumpled up worksheets, old permission slips... just a total mess. It was like a black hole in there. My teachers would literally have to make me stay inside during recess sometimes just to empty the whole thing out on the floor and sort through it because things were just getting lost in the abyss. 

So, yeah, when I think about it, this isn't really a new thing at all. It's just... it's just the adult version of it now, I guess. Instead of a desk stuffed with half-finished coloring pages, it's my email inbox and my client briefs, which is why it feels so much more stressful and embarrassing now that I'm supposed to be a professional. But the feeling itself? Yeah, that's been there since I was a little kid.

It’s just so frustrating because I want to stay put, I really do, and I tell myself beforehand that I'm going to just sit there, but my body is just like, \"nope, time to move,\" and then I'm out of my seat again before I even consciously decide to do it.\n\nDoctor: Do you also have trouble paying attention or staying focused?\n\nPatient: Oh, definitely. You know, it’s funny you ask that, because when people talk about these kinds of issues, I feel like everyone immediately pictures that one kid in class who is just literally bouncing off the walls, right? Like, my cousin Matthew was exactly like that when we were growing up. He could not stay in his seat to save his life, he was always getting up to sharpen his pencil fifty times a day, tapping his feet, swinging his legs. 

But for me... no, not really. I don't actually remember anyone ever using the word "fidgety" to describe me, and I don't think my parents ever got told I couldn't stay in my chair. Like I was saying before about those old report cards my mom kept in that big binder, the notes were always, always about me talking out of turn or rushing through my spelling tests or having a desk that looked like a natural disaster. But physically sitting in the chair? I was actually pretty okay at that. 

I would sit there during, say, Mrs. Gable’s math lessons—she was my fourth-grade teacher, the one who used to make me stay inside during recess to clean out my desk—and I’d be in my seat the entire time. I wasn't running around the room or squirming out of my chair. I was just... mentally completely somewhere else. I'd be sitting perfectly still, but I'd be staring out the window at the playground, or I'd be meticulously peeling the paper wrapper off my crayons piece by piece, or drawing these elaborate little stars all over the margins of my notebook. So I was contained to my desk, it was just that my brain was doing all the running around, if that makes sense? 

So, physically unable to sit still? No, I don't think so. No one ever really complained about my physical energy levels. I was actually pretty good at staying put, as long as I had someone sitting next to me to whisper to or something to daydream about while the teacher was talking.

Um... you know, it’s funny, because after just telling you how I blurt things out and interrupt people, you’d probably think the answer would be a huge yes. But actually... no. Not at all, really. 

When it comes to actual actions, like making decisions or doing things, I am the complete opposite of impulsive. I am a massive, massive overthinker. Like, if we're talking about making hasty decisions? I literally cannot do that. I agonize over every little choice. 

In my job, you know, doing advertising sales, there’s a lot of pressure to make quick calls on deals or negotiate on the fly, but I never just jump into things. I always have to take a step back, look at the client history, review the numbers... I'm very cautious about what I actually commit to.

I never just say, "Let's go here!" and walk in somewhere blindly. I just can't do it. 

And for bigger things? It's even worse. Like, I bought a new car last year, and I think I spent three entire months researching safety ratings, fuel efficiency, and depreciation values before I even allowed myself to set foot on a dealership lot. I had this massive color-coded spreadsheet with all the pros and cons of like, six different makes and models. I drove my boyfriend completely crazy because I just would not pull the trigger and make a choice. 

So, yeah, acting without thinking is definitely not me. It's weird, right? Because my mouth will just run off without my permission in a conversation, but if I actually have to take a physical action or make a choice, I freeze up and over-analyze every single possible outcome. So, no, I wouldn't say I do impulsive things at all. If anything, I take way, way too long to act.

I’ll just suddenly snap back to reality and realize I’ve been staring at the exact same PowerPoint slide—like, maybe a graph about Q3 ad spend—for what feels like ten minutes, and I have absolutely zero idea what the person at the front of the room just said. Nothing. It’s a complete blank. \n\nAnd it’s not just in meetings, either. It happens when I’m by myself at my desk, trying to read through a new client brief. These briefs are so important, you know? They have all the details about what the client wants for their campaign, their target demographics, their brand voice, all of that. I’ll start reading, and I’m reading the words, but after a paragraph or two, I realize I’m just moving my eyes across the page. I’m not absorbing a single thing. I’ll have to go back and re-read the same paragraph three, four, maybe five times before it actually sticks in my head. It’s exhausting, honestly. I feel like I’m working twice as hard just to keep up with the basic information everyone else seems to just absorb on the first try. It’s like my brain just decides it’s done paying attention, even when I really, really need it to.\n\nDoctor: Did these attention and restlessness problems start before you were 12 years old?\n\nPatient: Oh, wow, yeah. Absolutely. I mean, I remember this starting way, way before high school. Actually, it’s funny you ask about being younger than twelve, because my mom used to keep all my old report cards and teacher evaluations in this big binder, and every single parent-teacher conference in elementary school was pretty much the exact same conversation. \n\nThey would always write these notes saying that I was a really bright kid, which, you know, is nice to hear, but then there was always a \"but.\" It was always, \"she’s bright, but she rushes through everything.\" And the talking! I was constantly getting in trouble for talking out of turn. I just couldn't seem to hold my thoughts in—if the teacher asked a question, I’d just blurt out the answer before she even finished calling on someone else, or I'd be chatting with the kid next to me when we were supposed to be doing silent reading. \n\nAnd the homework situation was a constant battle. I was always forgetting my homework. Half the time I’d actually do it at home, but then I’d leave it on the kitchen counter, or I'd forget to even write down what the assignment was in the first place. And my desk... oh my gosh, my desk in like, third and fourth grade was a complete disaster zone. If you lifted the top, it was just stuffed to the absolute brim with half-finished papers, crumpled up worksheets, old permission slips... just a total mess. It was like a black hole in there. My teachers would literally have to make me stay inside during recess sometimes just to empty the whole thing out on the floor and sort through it because things were just getting lost in the abyss. \n\nSo, yeah, when I think about it, this isn't really a new thing at all. It's just... it's just the adult version of it now, I guess. Instead of a desk stuffed with half-finished coloring pages, it's my email inbox and my client briefs, which is why it feels so much more stressful and embarrassing now that I'm supposed to be a professional. But the feeling itself? Yeah, that's been there since I was a little kid.\n\nDoctor: Do you often interrupt other people before they finish speaking?\n\nPatient: Oh, god, yes. All the time. It’s actually one of the things I’m most self-conscious about, especially in my line of work where communication is literally everything. Like, I’ll be in a pitch or even just a casual catch-up with a client, and they’ll start asking a question—and my brain just immediately races ahead. I’ll think I know exactly where they’re going with it, so I just... I often just jump right in with an answer before a client or a coworker has even finished asking the question. \n\nAnd it’s so embarrassing because half the time, they finish their thought while I’m talking over them, and I realize I answered the completely wrong thing, or I just totally cut them off and derailed their whole point. \n\nLike, just last week, my manager was trying to ask me about the timeline for a digital campaign, and she goes, \"For the new social push, are we thinking—\" and I just instantly blurted out, \"Yes, the graphics are done!\" And she just stared at me, took this long breath, and said, \"...are we thinking of launching on Tuesday or Wednesday?\" I just wanted the floor to swallow me whole. \n\nI do it with clients, too, which is obviously even worse. They’ll be asking about target demographics and I’m already spitting out pricing options before they even hit the question mark at the end of their sentence. I can see them get this slight look on their face, like, \"Did she really just interrupt me?\" And I know how incredibly rude it comes across! I really do. It’s not that I don’t value what they’re saying or that I'm not listening, it’s just like my mouth is moving faster than my impulse control. The words are already out there in the air before I can tell myself to just bite my tongue, take a breath, and wait my turn. It makes me seem so impatient and scattered, and I just... I hate it, but I can't seem to stop doing it no matter how much I tell myself to just wait for people to finish speaking.\n\nDoctor: When you were a child, did teachers or adults often describe you as fidgety or unable to sit still?\n\nPatient: You know, it’s funny you ask that, because when people talk about these kinds of issues, I feel like everyone immediately pictures that one kid in class who is just literally bouncing off the walls, right? Like, my cousin Matthew was exactly like that when we were growing up. He could not stay in his seat to save his life, he was always getting up to sharpen his pencil fifty times a day, tapping his feet, swinging his legs. \n\nBut for me... no, not really. I don't actually remember anyone ever using the word \"fidgety\" to describe me, and I don't think my parents ever got told I couldn't stay in my chair. Like I was saying before about those old report cards my mom kept in that big binder, the notes were always, always about me talking out of turn or rushing through my spelling tests or having a desk that looked like a natural disaster. But physically sitting in the chair? I was actually pretty okay at that. \n\nI would sit there during, say, Mrs. Gable’s math lessons—she was my fourth-grade teacher, the one who used to make me stay inside during recess to clean out my desk—and I’d be in my seat the entire time. I wasn't running around the room or squirming out of my chair. I was just... mentally completely somewhere else. I'd be sitting perfectly still, but I'd be staring out the window at the playground, or I'd be meticulously peeling the paper wrapper off my crayons piece by piece, or drawing these elaborate little stars all over the margins of my notebook. If we're trying to figure out where to go for dinner on a Friday night, I will spend forty-five minutes reading Yelp reviews, looking at the menus, checking the distance on Google Maps, cross-referencing everything before I can even suggest a place. I never just say, \"Let's go here!\" and walk in somewhere blindly. I just can't do it. \n\nAnd for bigger things? It's even worse. I had this massive color-coded spreadsheet with all the pros and cons of like, six different makes and models. I drove my boyfriend completely crazy because I just would not pull the trigger and make a choice. \n\nSo, yeah, acting without thinking is definitely not me. It's weird, right? Because my mouth will just run off without my permission in a conversation, but if I actually have to take a physical action or make a choice, I freeze up and over-analyze every single possible outcome. So, no, I wouldn't say I do impulsive things at all. If anything, I take way, way too long to act.\n\nDoctor: Do you often feel physically restless, like you need to move or can’t stay seated?\n\nPatient: You know, it’s interesting because I just said I wasn’t a fidgety kid, but as an adult... yeah, actually. My coworker actually joked about it recently, asking if I was trying to get my daily steps in during the Q3 review. I laughed it off, but inside I was just so frustrated with myself. I just think, *Why can't I sit normally like a professional adult?* It’s just this overwhelming, restless urge to move, and half the time I’m sitting there just strategizing about when it’s socially acceptable for me to stand up again instead of actually listening to the revenue targets. Oh, wow, yes. Absolutely. I know I mentioned earlier about blurting things out and interrupting, but just the sheer volume of talking? Yeah, that is a massive thing for me. 

It’s actually really embarrassing, especially because in my line of work, obviously, you have to be a good communicator. You're selling, you're pitching, you have to be enthusiastic. It's almost like this weird out-of-body experience where a little voice in the back of my head is going, *Okay, you made the point, wrap it up, let someone else talk,* but my mouth just completely ignores it. I just can't seem to find a natural stopping point because every new thought feels so incredibly urgent and connected to the last one, and I'm terrified I'll forget it if I don't say it right that second. 

So I just keep going and going, and by the time I finally force myself to stop and actually take a breath, the energy in the room has totally shifted. I look around the table, and I can just tell that the rest of my team—like the creative director or the account manager—were literally just sitting there, completely stalled out, waiting for a chance to speak. You can see it in their body language, you know? They’ll have their hands raised slightly or their mouths half-open, just waiting for a gap in my monologue that never came. It makes me feel so guilty because I don't want to steamroll anyone, I really don't, but once I get going on an idea, I just... I don't know how to hit the brakes.

I'll find absolutely any excuse to leave my chair, even if it’s just to refill my water bottle for the third time in an hour, or sometimes I'll just go stand and pace by the printer in the corner like I'm waiting for a document that doesn't even exist. My coworkers are starting to give me these looks, and I just feel so unprofessional because I'm thirty years old and I should be able to sit through a strategy session without needing to wander around the room. It’s just so frustrating because I want to stay put, I really do, and I tell myself beforehand that I'm going to just sit there, but my body is just like, \"nope, time to move,\" and then I'm out of my seat again before I even consciously decide to do it.\n\nDoctor: Do you also have trouble paying attention or staying focused?\n\nPatient: Oh, definitely. Yes. It's actually a huge problem, and it kind of ties into the whole meeting thing I was just talking about. Like, I’ll be in those same strategy meetings, right? And I go in with the best intentions. I’ve got my notebook out, my favorite pen, I’ve had my coffee, and I’m looking right at the presenter. I’m thinking, \"Okay, we are going to nail these quarterly projections.\" And for the first few minutes, I’m totally locked in. I’m following the numbers, I’m nodding along. \n\nBut then... it’s like someone just unplugs a cord in my brain. I won’t even realize it’s happening at first. I’ll just suddenly snap back to reality and realize I’ve been staring at the exact same PowerPoint slide—like, maybe a graph about Q3 ad spend—for what feels like ten minutes, and I have absolutely zero idea what the person at the front of the room just said. Nothing. It’s a complete blank. \n\nAnd it’s not just in meetings, either. It happens when I’m by myself at my desk, trying to read through a new client brief. These briefs are so important, you know? They have all the details about what the client wants for their campaign, their target demographics, their brand voice, all of that. I’ll start reading, and I’m reading the words, but after a paragraph or two, I realize I’m just moving my eyes across the page. I’m not absorbing a single thing. I’ll have to go back and re-read the same paragraph three, four, maybe five times before it actually sticks in my head. It’s exhausting, honestly. I feel like I’m working twice as hard just to keep up with the basic information everyone else seems to just absorb on the first try. It’s like my brain just decides it’s done paying attention, even when I really, really need it to.\n\nDoctor: Did these attention and restlessness problems start before you were 12 years old?\n\nPatient: Oh, wow, yeah. Absolutely. I mean, I remember this starting way, way before high school. Actually, it’s funny you ask about being younger than twelve, because my mom used to keep all my old report cards and teacher evaluations in this big binder, and every single parent-teacher conference in elementary school was pretty much the exact same conversation. \n\nThey would always write these notes saying that I was a really bright kid, which, you know, is nice to hear, but then there was always a \"but.\" It was always, \"she’s bright, but she rushes through everything.\" And the talking! I was always forgetting my homework. Half the time I’d actually do it at home, but then I’d leave it on the kitchen counter, or I'd forget to even write down what the assignment was in the first place. The words are already out there in the air before I can tell myself to just bite my tongue, take a breath, and wait my turn. It makes me seem so impatient and scattered, and I just... I hate it, but I can't seem to stop doing it no matter how much I tell myself to just wait for people to finish speaking.\n\nDoctor: When you were a child, did teachers or adults often describe you as fidgety or unable to sit still?\n\nPatient: You know, it’s funny you ask that, because when people talk about these kinds of issues, I feel like everyone immediately pictures that one kid in class who is just literally bouncing off the walls, right? So, no, I wouldn't say I do impulsive things at all. If anything, I take way, way too long to act.\n\nDoctor: Do you often feel physically restless, like you need to move or can’t stay seated?\n\nPatient: You know, it’s interesting because I just said I wasn’t a fidgety kid, but as an adult... yeah, actually. Honestly, no, not at all. It’s so funny because when you hear about this kind of thing, you always picture the little boy bouncing off the walls, driving the teacher crazy, right? But that just wasn't me. I was the exact opposite of that kid.

Oh, it's definitely not just my mind drifting. I mean, my mind does drift, obviously, but the feeling of needing to get up is so... physical. It's like this actual, tangible sensation in my body, almost like a buzzing or a tightness in my chest and my legs. 

It’s not just that I’m bored and thinking about what I’m going to have for lunch, it’s that my body is literally screaming at me to move. It’s almost painful, in a weird way. Not like a sharp pain, but just this overwhelming, unbearable discomfort. I try so hard to suppress it. I’ll dig my fingernails into my palms under the table, or I’ll bounce my heel, just trying to release some of that energy without actually getting up, but it never really works. It’s like trying to hold the lid on a pot of boiling water. Eventually, the pressure just gets to be too much, and I have to find some excuse—any excuse—to stand up, even if it's just for thirty seconds. So, yeah, it's very much a physical inability to just stay put, not just me zoning out.

Oh, gosh, yes. Losing things is practically my part-time job at this point. It’s actually become a running joke in the office, which is... well, it’s funny sometimes, but mostly it’s just incredibly stressful. I’m constantly, and I mean *constantly*, hunting for things I need for work.

It’s just... it’s exhausting. It feels like I spend half my day just trying to locate the basic tools I need to do my job, and by the time I actually find them, I’m so flustered and behind schedule that I can’t even focus on the task itself. Because my mouth will just run off without my permission in a conversation, but if I actually have to take a physical action or make a choice, I freeze up and over-analyze every single possible outcome. So, no, I wouldn't say I do impulsive things at all. If anything, I take way, way too long to act.\n\nDoctor: Do you often feel physically restless, like you need to move or can’t stay seated?\n\nPatient: You know, it’s interesting because I just said I wasn’t a fidgety kid, but as an adult... yeah, actually. Honestly, that specific thing is a huge part of what finally made me come in to see you. It’s become a real issue at work. \n\nIn my agency, we have these massive, sprawling sales strategy meetings—they can go on for two, sometimes three hours at a time. We’re all packed into this big glass conference room, the VP of Sales is at the head of the table going over quarterly projections, and everyone else is just sitting there, perfectly fine, taking notes on their laptops. But me? I just cannot stay in my chair. \n\nAfter about forty-five minutes, I get this... this literal physical itch in my legs. I know I’m supposed to stay seated. It’s a formal meeting! I just think, *Why can't I sit normally like a professional adult?* It’s just this overwhelming, restless urge to move, and half the time I’m sitting there just strategizing about when it’s socially acceptable for me to stand up again instead of actually listening to the revenue targets. You're selling, you're pitching, you have to be enthusiastic. I get so fired up. I’ll be presenting our angle, and I just get completely swept up in the campaign idea. I'll start explaining the core concept, and then I'll veer off into how we can adapt the messaging for different social platforms, and then I'll start detailing the exact kind of imagery we should use, and... it just snowballs. \n\nAnd the worst part is, while I'm doing it, I can actually hear myself going on way too long. It's almost like this weird out-of-body experience where a little voice in the back of my head is going, *Okay, you made the point, wrap it up, let someone else talk,* but my mouth just completely ignores it. I just can't seem to find a natural stopping point because every new thought feels so incredibly urgent and connected to the last one, and I'm terrified I'll forget it if I don't say it right that second. \n\nSo I just keep going and going, and by the time I finally force myself to stop and actually take a breath, the energy in the room has totally shifted. I look around the table, and I can just tell that the rest of my team—like the creative director or the account manager—were literally just sitting there, completely stalled out, waiting for a chance to speak. You can see it in their body language, you know? They’ll have their hands raised slightly or their mouths half-open, just waiting for a gap in my monologue that never came. It makes me feel so guilty because I don't want to steamroll anyone, I really don't, but once I get going on an idea, I just... It was just never on anyone's radar.\n\nDoctor: When you’re in situations where you have to stay seated, do you actually feel physically unable to remain in your seat, or is it mostly that your mind drifts off?\n\nPatient: Oh, it's definitely not just my mind drifting. Bouncing off the walls... well, maybe not literally scaling the walls like Spiderman, but... yeah, I definitely remember this whole thing starting way, way before high school. 

Like, if you look back at my elementary school report cards—my mom actually kept all of them in this giant plastic storage bin in her attic, she's very sentimental like that—my teachers always wrote the exact same kinds of things. They’d always start by saying I was bright, which was nice, I guess, a good way to soften the blow for my parents. But then the rest of the paragraph would just be this laundry list of things I was doing wrong. They'd always say I rushed through all my work, just totally speeding through assignments so I could be the first one done, which meant my handwriting was a mess and I made a ton of silly mistakes. 

And, like I was saying earlier about Mrs. Gable, they always noted that I talked out of turn. Just constantly blurting things out. But it wasn't just the physical energy or the talking, it was the absolute chaos that followed me around. I constantly forgot my homework. I would literally sit at the kitchen table with my mom, do the entire math worksheet, and then somehow it would just vanish from my brain the next morning and never make it into my backpack. 

And my desk! Oh my gosh, my desk at school was a literal hazard zone. It was just stuffed completely full of half-finished papers, crinkled up worksheets, old permission slips... you'd lift the little wooden lid and it would all just sort of spring out at you because I had shoved so much stuff in there just to get it out of sight. I never actually finished anything before moving on to the next thing. So, I don't know if they used the exact phrase 'bouncing off the walls' to describe me, but I was definitely a very rushed, chaotic, non-stop kind of kid from a very, very young age. It's actually kind of wild to think about how early it all started, now that we're talking about it.

If I try to force myself to stay perfectly still, it almost physically hurts, like my muscles get all tight and my skin starts to feel like it's itching. We'll be trying to watch a movie and I'm getting up a million times to check my phone in the kitchen, or I'm shaking the entire sofa because my leg is bouncing. He always ends up just putting his hand heavily on my knee to get me to stop, which is sweet of him to not yell at me, but it definitely makes me feel a bit guilty that I can't just relax with him. \n\nBut honestly? Where it's really, really becoming a massive issue—and this is what's actually keeping me up at night and making me so incredibly anxious lately—is at work. I look around the table, and I can just tell that the rest of my team—like the creative director or the account manager—were literally just sitting there, completely stalled out, waiting for a chance to speak. You can see it in their body language, you know? They’ll have their hands raised slightly or their mouths half-open, just waiting for a gap in my monologue that never came. It makes me feel so guilty because I don't want to steamroll anyone, I really don't, but once I get going on an idea, I just... I don't know how to hit the brakes.\n\nDoctor: As a child, did you often leave your seat when you were expected to stay seated?\n\nPatient: As a child? Um, actually, no. I really wasn't like that back then. I was always pretty good about staying at my desk. I mean, I went to this somewhat strict elementary school where they were super big on classroom rules, so you just didn't get up unless you raised your hand and asked for permission. I was way too much of a rule-follower to break that, so I'd just sit there. \n\nBut... well, it’s exactly like I was literally just telling you a minute ago. It's like this actual, tangible sensation in my body, almost like a buzzing or a tightness in my chest and my legs. \n\nIt’s not just that I’m bored and thinking about what I’m going to have for lunch, it’s that my body is literally screaming at me to move.
